text:
The Rangers scored first on a power play and then spent the rest of the night chasing a game Washington controlled. Alexis Lafrenière's snap shot at 10:17 of the first, set up by J.T. Miller and Pavel Dorofeyev, was the only puck to beat Logan Thompson, who stopped 21 of 22 and saved nearly two goals more than the chances warranted. Washington's expected goals total of 4.48 against 2.89 for New York says the Capitals were the better team, and the simulated replays agree, though only modestly: they gave Washington the win 55 percent of the time.

The turn came in the second. Timothy Liljegren tied it at 6:08 with a slap shot that had only a 3 percent chance of going in, a goal more about timing than quality. Boone Jenner then put Washington ahead at 17:38, and his 0.54 individual expected goals show how often he got into dangerous ice. Washington generated 1.35 expected goals in that period to New York's 0.87. The Rangers' goaltending kept them close, with Igor Shesterkin and Dylan Garand each allowing one goal, but neither could be faulted much for the deficit.

The final push belonged to Washington. Its 1.90 expected goals in the third was the largest single-period gap on either side, and Tom Wilson sealed it at 19:59 with a wrist shot that carried an 84 percent chance of scoring. Wilson finished with 1.21 individual expected goals, far above anyone else in the building. Both teams took three penalties, but New York's single power-play goal was all it managed. Shot attempts were nearly even, 51 to 50, so Washington's edge came from chance quality and Thompson's work, not volume.
